title: K-T-N

lines: A HORN OF OIL IN BETHLEHEM.
cards: A prophet stands in a farmhouse in Bethlehem with a horn of oil, looking for a king. The farmer, Jesse, brings out his sons, one after another, tall ones, impressive ones. Each time the answer is no.
Finally the prophet asks whether these are all the children. Jesse says, in effect, well, there's still the youngest, out with the sheep. In Hebrew he calls him ha-katan.
The small one. Nobody thought to invite him. That small one is David.

teach.b: K-T-N. Kuf, tet, nun. Katan: small, little, young.
First, the sky. Yesterday's root sits in Genesis next to today's: God made the two great lights, "the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night." The greater is gadol.
The lesser is katan. A midrash in the Talmud tells that the moon objected to sharing the sky as an equal, and was told to make itself smaller.
Then, the story goes, the moon was comforted: the righteous would be called by its name, David the small.
So the small light and the small boy end up in the same story. Second, Jacob.
On his way home, afraid of his brother, he prays, and the Hebrew has him say katonti, I am small, before all the kindness and truth God has shown him.
A man with flocks and two camps of people, saying: I'm too small for all this.
Third, the prophet Zechariah, watching a modest rebuilding that looked like nothing: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The word for small things is from this root. Fourth, the street.
In Jewish law, a katan is a minor, a child not yet obligated in the commandments.

teach.h: A LIGHT COMMANDMENT, HANDLED WITH CARE.
teach.b: And the sayings of the fathers teach to be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, because you don't know the reward of each.
Small doesn't mean it doesn't count. Small is often where it starts.

how: Jewish teaching often turns to katan, small: the Talmud's story of the moon made smaller, Jacob's katonti, and the teaching in Pirkei Avot to treat a light commandment as carefully as a weighty one.

games.q: you're Jesse. a prophet wants to see your sons. your youngest is out with the sheep. what do you do?
o: bring out the older sons and leave the small one in the field.
games.why: Jesse brings out the older sons. only when the prophet asks does he mention ha-katan, the small one. it's David.

practice: Look around for something small that does a job nobody thanks it for, a button, a hinge, a light switch, and rest your eyes on it for a few breaths.
Then widen it to a person: someone easy to overlook in your day, whose name you may barely know, who keeps things running. If you pray, you can say a word of thanks for them.
